claims.text: The initial material is a single-phase, coarse-grained CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy.
Resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion is governed by a dynamically induced ultra-nanocrystalline surface layer.
Mechanical sliding causes dynamic amorphization in coarse-grained CoCrFeMnNi.
Dynamic amorphization refines the near-surface microstructure into an ultra-nanocrystalline layer.
The ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer has reduced shear strength through inverse Hall-Petch behavior.
Formation of the ultra-nanocrystalline layer is linked to low friction in CoCrFeMnNi.
Formation of the ultra-nanocrystalline layer is linked to high wear resistance in CoCrFeMnNi under inert conditions.
The ultra-nanocrystalline layer promotes formation of a stable, self-healing passive oxide film.
The passive oxide film retards corrosive attack.
Under corrosive sliding, CoCrFeMnNi will have lower wear volume than under matched inert sliding.
Under corrosive sliding, CoCrFeMnNi will have lower corrosion current density than the inert-environment baseline.
Combined wear-corrosion degradation will be less severe than the sum of separately measured wear and corrosion degradation.
Continuous renewal of the ultra-nanocrystalline layer passivates newly exposed surfaces during sliding.
The proposed protection should operate at moderate loads and sliding speeds that permit formation of the ultra-nanocrystalline layer.
Extreme loads or temperatures can prevent formation of, or rapidly break down, the ultra-nanocrystalline layer.
Pre-existing microstructural defects can inhibit dynamic amorphization.
Prior evidence supports low wear under inert conditions in association with dynamic amorphization and near-surface refinement.
The quantitative effect of the layer on passivation during combined wear and corrosion is not established and may depend on corrosive medium and stress conditions.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis proposes comparing corrosion current density against an inert-atmosphere baseline, but an inert, non-aqueous wear test does not provide a directly comparable electrochemical corrosion current. A matched chloride-electrolyte corrosion-only or open-circuit control would be needed for that comparison.
